channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Japan's core consumer price inflation rose to 2.1% year on year in September from 1.7% in August, above the Bank of Japan's 2% target for the first time in nine months, Channel News Asia reports.
item.description:
Channel News Asia reports that Japan's core consumer price index, which excludes fresh food but includes fuel, rose 2.1% year on year in September, from 1.7% in August, the first time in nine months that annual core inflation has been above the 2% target set by the Bank of Japan. The row says the figures underscored how higher fuel costs from the prolonged Middle East conflict, price pressures from robust AI demand and elevated import prices driven by the weak yen were blunting the effect of government fuel subsidies. It adds that the Bank of Japan is set to leave policy unchanged next week but may raise its inflation forecast and signal readiness to keep raising still-low borrowing costs. The row does not give headline inflation, the contribution of fuel, food or services, wage data or the date of the Bank's decision.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives one inflation measure and an expectation for the central bank, not a decision. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, inflation above target together with a weak yen and high fuel costs increases the likelihood of further rate rises, which raise borrowing costs for construction and capital spending. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Japan is a market for industrial and construction materials and a base for automotive and electronics customers, so a weak yen and higher rates could change import costs and investment plans in different directions, and the row gives no figure for either. Points that may be worth considering include the Bank of Japan's decision and its forecast revision, the yen, and the future of the fuel subsidies.

Channel News Asia

item.title: The IMF's regional outlook projects output in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan down 1.3% in 2026 and up 6.6% in 2027 if the war subsides in early 2027, and Saudi Arabia's real GDP down 3.3% in 2026.
item.description:
Asharq Al-Awsat reports that Jihad Azour, director of the IMF's Middle East and Central Asia Department, said the war in the Middle East was weighing on the region's outlook through energy, shipping, tourism, trade and confidence, and that the IMF's Regional Economic Outlook assumes the conflict subsides in early 2027 and trade gradually returns to normal. Under that scenario the economies of the Middle East and North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan are projected to contract by 1.3% in 2026 and to grow by 6.6% in 2027. Lianhe Zaobao adds that the 2027 level would still be below pre-war forecasts, that oil-exporting countries directly affected by disrupted production and shipping have suffered most, that oil importers have been more resilient, and that the outlook could worsen if energy production is disrupted further. For Saudi Arabia, Asharq Al-Awsat reports a projected 3.3% fall in real GDP in 2026, because hydrocarbon activity declined in the first half amid disruptions to energy production, shipping and supply chains, particularly those linked to the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, with non-oil activity more resilient, and projected real GDP growth of 7.9% in 2027 as energy production gradually returns to normal and security and trade conditions improve. The rows do not give forecasts for other countries, the pre-war forecast levels, or trade or petrochemical volumes.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give IMF projections that rest on a stated assumption about the end of the conflict, not outcomes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a contraction followed by a strong rebound that depends on the war subsiding leaves regional demand for construction and industrial goods uncertain, and disrupted energy production and shipping can affect supply from the region. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the Middle East is both a source of petrochemical raw materials and a market for construction and industrial materials, so lower regional output could weigh on project demand while disrupted energy and shipping could affect raw-material supply, and the rows give no petrochemical or construction figures. Points that may be worth considering include whether the conflict subsides as the baseline assumes, the IMF's next update, and Gulf petrochemical export volumes.

Asharq Al-Awsat | Asharq Al-Awsat (Saudi Arabia) | Lianhe Zaobao | Business Recorder

item.title: The premium investors demand on French government bonds over German Bunds widened to 177.7 basis points on 22 October, the widest since November 2011, the Globe and Mail reports.
item.description:
The Globe and Mail reports that on 22 October the premium investors demand to hold French government debt over German Bunds widened, with the spread reaching 177.7 basis points, the widest since November 2011, during the euro zone debt crisis. It says this underscored investor unease about France's fiscal outlook and that the sell-off in French bonds has been driven by political uncertainty ahead of the 2027 presidential election and difficulties in passing a budget. It quotes Nomura's senior European economist Andrzej Szczepaniak as saying that the key question is whether the European Central Bank would intervene if market tensions intensify. A Commercial Times row published the evening before gives the 10-year spread as 159.4 basis points on 21 October, described as a 15-year high, with the 10-year yield briefly above 5%, a high since 2002, and says the French government is trying to pass a 2027 budget with about EUR 43 billion of deficit-reduction measures amid divisions in parliament. The rows do not say whether the two spread figures use the same benchmark bonds or time of day, give the French or German yield levels on 22 October, or report any ECB action.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a market spread and one economist's question, not a policy decision. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a wider spread means higher borrowing costs for the French state and can pass into the funding costs of French banks and companies, with the budget outcome and any ECB response deciding whether it persists. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, France is a large market for construction and industrial products, so higher public and private funding costs could weigh on public investment and construction financing, while the rows give no figure for either. Points that may be worth considering include progress of the French budget, statements by the ECB, and mortgage and corporate borrowing costs in France and the euro area.

Globe and Mail | Commercial Times

item.title: Companies and governments rushed to patch critical flaws in the PHP programming language on 22 October, after precautionary website shutdowns on 21 October, as a cybersecurity company reported millions of hacking attempts.
item.description:
The Straits Times and Arab News report that on 22 October companies and governments around the world rushed to patch critical flaws in PHP, a widely used programming language, as a cybersecurity company (in Arab News's wording, a cloud firm) reported millions of hacking attempts after the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Governments in Europe and elsewhere took websites offline as a precaution on 21 October; the rows describe emergency shutdowns of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services from Tokyo to Helsinki. The Independent reports that the UK tech minister confirmed 32 UK government services are temporarily offline and four are partially unavailable, that PHP powers almost 70% of websites according to Cloudflare, and that No 10 said no major public-facing critical systems had been affected. MarketScreener reports that the Office for Budget Responsibility took its website down after cyber security chiefs warned UK organisations that the flaw could allow attackers to take remote control of any web servers running PHP, and the National Cyber Security Centre urged organisations to update or consider taking sites offline if they cannot be upgraded immediately, and that the Scotland Secretary said the security of the forthcoming Budget was not compromised. The Hindu Business Line reports that PHP contains two vulnerabilities, that its maintainers released updates on Wednesday and that the US Office of the National Cyber Director was coordinating with the FBI and other federal security agencies. The rows report attempts and precautionary shutdowns. They do not name an organisation that was breached, say how long services stayed offline, or give any effect on manufacturers.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give an emergency response and attack attempts, not confirmed damage. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a flaw in software that runs most websites exposes any organisation that operates customer portals, ordering systems or supplier platforms, and precautionary shutdowns can interrupt business until patches are applied. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, chemical producers and their customers and logistics partners operate web portals and ordering and tracking systems, so shutdowns or intrusions could delay order handling, shipments or customs documents for a time; the rows name no manufacturer or logistics service. Points that may be worth considering include the patch status of own and suppliers' web systems, outages at logistics, customs or banking portals, and reports of successful intrusions.

Straits Times | Arab News | Independent | MarketScreener | Hindu Business Line

item.title: Negotiators from EU member states and the European Parliament have agreed to raise the limit above which the emissions-trading reserve cancels certificates from 400 million to up to 700 million, Frankfurter Rundschau reports.
item.description:
Frankfurter Rundschau reports that negotiators from EU member states and the European Parliament have agreed on a targeted adjustment of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), with the aim of preventing extreme price fluctuations and unpredictable cost jumps. The row describes the Market Stability Reserve as the mechanism that takes in unused certificates when the economy weakens and factories produce less, so that the price does not fall sharply, and releases them again when the economy recovers and a shortage threatens, so that the price does not jump. Until now, the row says, this protection was limited by a fixed upper limit of 400 million units: certificates above that threshold were automatically declared invalid and permanently deleted, so they were lost for later crises. The negotiators agreed on a middle course. The limit will not be completely abolished, but the threshold for the invalidation mechanism will be significantly raised, and up to 700 million certificates may remain in the reserve in future. The row does not say whether the Council and the Parliament still have to adopt the agreement formally, when it would apply, how many certificates the reserve holds today, what a certificate costs or how industry would be affected.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row describes a rule change on how many certificates the reserve may keep, not a price or a cost. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a reserve that can hold more certificates can release more of them in a shortage, which would dampen spikes in the carbon price, with the effect depending on how many certificates enter the reserve and on market conditions. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the chemical industry is covered by the emissions trading system and some of its raw materials and energy carry a carbon cost, so a more predictable carbon cost could ease planning for producers and for their suppliers, while the row gives no figure for either. Points that may be worth considering include formal adoption of the agreement, the number of certificates in the reserve, and how carbon costs are passed into raw-material prices.

Frankfurter Rundschau

item.title: Piyush Goyal, India's commerce minister, says the India–EU free trade agreement will be signed by the end of 2026 and may take effect in the first quarter of 2027, and calls the EU's carbon border tax "inviting disaster".
item.description:
Business Standard reports that India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal announced that the free trade agreement with the European Union will be signed by the end of 2026 and may come into effect in the first quarter of 2027; he is on a six-day visit to Germany and the Netherlands. The New Indian Express reports that on 22 October he said the pact could come into force in the next four to five months, urged businesses on both sides to start exchanging product samples and discussing quality requirements and prices, and called for a trade target between India and Germany of EUR 310 billion, against about EUR 31 billion now. The Economic Times and LiveMint report that at the Berlin Global Dialogue on 22 October he warned the EU that its carbon border adjustment mechanism, a tax on carbon-intensive imported goods, and a growing list of regulations could raise costs, stoke inflation and weaken the bloc's competitiveness. LiveMint adds that he said a 50% import duty on steel would raise the cost of living and that EU industry would be out-priced, and that New Delhi has secured EU commitments, among them an assurance that any flexibilities granted to third countries under the mechanism will also be extended to India. All four rows report the minister's own statements. None gives an EU confirmation of the signing date, the tariff terms of the agreement, its coverage of chemicals or plastics, or the rate or full product scope of the carbon border tax.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give the Indian minister's account of timing and his criticism, not the terms of the agreement. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a signed agreement between two large markets would change tariffs and market access over time, while disputes over carbon-related import charges can complicate the timetable. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, India is a growing market for construction and manufacturing materials and the EU a large supplier and market, so tariff changes on chemicals and on goods that contain adhesives could change trade flows between the two regions, and a carbon charge on steel imports could affect the cost of steel-based products; the rows give no tariff schedule or figures. Points that may be worth considering include the agreement text on chemicals and rules of origin, an EU confirmation of the signing date, and how the carbon charge treats Indian exports.

Business Standard | New Indian Express | Economic Times | LiveMint

item.title: The state VDMA says machinery orders in Baden-Württemberg were 11% higher than a year earlier in the first eight months of 2026, after four years of declining orders, and expects sales to grow about 1% to EUR 84 billion this year.
item.description:
Wallstreet:online reports that machinery manufacturers in Baden-Württemberg are again reporting growing orders after four years of declining orders. According to the state association of the VDMA in Stuttgart, incoming orders in the first eight months of the year were 11% higher than in the same period last year, the first rise since the previous weak phase. Companies involved in the expansion of AI infrastructure or active in defence and aerospace particularly benefited. Sales also show signs of recovery: after two years of shrinkage, the VDMA expects them to grow by about 1% to a total of EUR 84 billion this year. More than half of the machinery companies now expect rising sales, and only one in five still expects a decline. The row does not give orders by customer industry or by domestic and foreign buyers, the size of the orders in euros, the national picture, or any figure for construction or automotive customers.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives order intake and an expected sales total for one state, not national figures. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, order growth that particularly benefits suppliers to AI infrastructure and defence would point to demand in specific niches rather than a broad recovery, and order intake usually leads output by some months. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, machinery and equipment manufacturers are customers for adhesive technologies, so rising orders could lift volumes at plants in the state with a lag, although if growth sits in a few niches the effect may be narrow, and the row gives no figure for materials. Points that may be worth considering include national order data for the sector when published, the split of orders by customer industry, and whether sales reach the expected EUR 84 billion.

Wallstreet:online

item.title: Handelsblatt reports that from 2027 German banks will have to hold less equity for residential construction loans, with the federal government wanting to free capital for housing finance.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that, starting from 2027, banks in Germany will have to hold less equity for residential construction loans. The row says the federal government wants to free up capital that banks can increasingly use to finance residential construction in future. It adds that some financial influencers, described as "finfluencers", are already deriving significantly falling construction interest rates from the change, and that some of them predict a new wave of rising valuations, because buyers could again afford higher purchase prices with cheaper loans. The row attributes these rate and price expectations only to the influencers. The row does not give the size of the reduction in the equity requirement, the legal instrument or whether the decision is final, which banks or loan types are covered, the effect on mortgage rates, or any construction volume.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a plan with a start year and a purpose, not a measured effect. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a lower equity requirement reduces the capital a bank must tie up for each loan, which can increase the volume of lending or lower its price, although banks' own decisions and interest rates set elsewhere also matter. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, residential construction is a customer segment, so easier financing of construction loans could support building starts and renovation work, and with them demand for adhesive technologies, after a lag, while the row gives no figure for lending or building activity. Points that may be worth considering include the size and legal status of the change, mortgage-rate and lending data after 2027, and building permits and starts.

Handelsblatt

item.title: ACEA data show EU new-car registrations rose 9.3% year on year to 971,048 in September, with battery-electric registrations up 72.9% to 290,117.
item.description:
Hürriyet Daily News, citing the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA), reports that new passenger car registrations in the European Union totalled 971,048 units in September, up 9.3% year on year, and that battery-electric registrations were 290,117 units, up 72.9%. It adds that in September Tesla and BYD registrations rose 78.6% and 111.4% to 45,866 and 28,309 units, with Tesla's market share rising from 2.9% to 4.7% and BYD's from 1.5% to 2.9%. For the first nine months it gives Tesla registrations of 188,035 (up 68.9%) and BYD registrations of 206,002 (up 154.4%), with market shares of 2.2% (from 1.4%) and 2.4% (from 1%). Channel News Asia, citing ACEA data for a wider area, reports that registrations across the EU, Britain and the European Free Trade Association reached 1.36 million in September, up 10.2%, and that battery-electric, plug-in hybrid and hybrid registrations rose 59.9%, 24% and 5.3% and together made up 76.2% of all new vehicles. MarketScreener, also citing ACEA, gives Tesla's September registrations as 68,776 units, up 72.5%, across the EU, the UK, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland; the Hürriyet figure of 45,866 units, up 78.6%, differs in size and growth rate, and the rows do not say that it covers the same area. The rows do not give registrations by fuel type outside electrified models, figures by country, or the nine-month EU total.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give ACEA registration counts, which measure vehicles sold, not vehicles built in Europe or demand for components. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a rise of about a tenth in registrations together with a large rise in battery-electric cars points to higher demand for passenger cars and a changing mix, and a rising share for Tesla and BYD can change which vehicle platforms and suppliers are specified. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle assembly and electric-vehicle batteries use adhesive technologies, so higher sales and a shift to electric models could raise volumes and change which products are qualified, with the effect depending on where the vehicles are built, and the rows give no production or materials figures. Points that may be worth considering include ACEA's production and country data, the share of imported models in registrations, and the trend in plug-in hybrid and hybrid sales.

Hürriyet Daily News | Channel News Asia | MarketScreener

item.title: The US said it ordered non-emergency government staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia over continuing Houthi threats, and oil rose more than USD 2 on 22 October, with ING analysts putting ICE Brent back above USD 110 a barrel.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that Saudi Arabian authorities blamed Iran-backed Houthi militants for an attack on a civilian airport that caused casualties, and that the US said it ordered non-emergency US government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia in response to continuing threats from the Yemen-based group. It adds that Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said on X that the country intercepted a drone that tried to target Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field on Wednesday. The row cites the Wall Street Journal, quoting officials familiar with the planning, as saying that the US military has been preparing a range of options to strike Iran, and says that President Trump has said the US will not attack Iran before the US midterm elections on 3 November; two aircraft carrier strike groups are in the Middle East, with a third on its way from the Pacific. The Straits Times reports that oil prices rallied by more than USD 2 a barrel on 22 October after more Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia raised concern about a wider escalation and further disruption to crude supplies. It says ING analysts put ICE Brent back above USD 110 that morning after additional deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia, and that US officials told Reuters the State Department plans to withdraw family members from a number of other US missions in the region. The rows do not give the number of casualties, any damage at the airport or the Shaybah field, any change in Saudi production or exports, the benchmark behind the USD 2 rise, or a date for any US action.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report attacks, a US departure order and a price move, not a change in oil supply. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, attacks on Saudi territory and a US order to reduce its presence raise the perceived risk to supply from the region and can lift oil prices, freight and insurance costs even without a loss of output. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, crude oil and gas are the base of many raw materials and of energy costs, so a sustained higher oil price or a disruption to Gulf exports could raise input costs with a delay, while the rows give no figures for petrochemicals. Points that may be worth considering include whether Saudi exports or Aramco facilities are affected, the Brent level in coming sessions, any US decision on action against Iran after 3 November, and freight and insurance costs for Gulf cargoes.

MarketScreener | Straits Times
